references.text: Jesus speaks of days coming when the bridegroom will be taken from them, and then they will fast – a parallel to the disciples longing for the days of the Son of Man ([ref:Luk 5:35|Luke 5:35]).
In the eschatological discourse, Jesus says that days will come when not one stone will be left upon another, a similar formulation about coming times of distress ([ref:Luk 21:6|Luke 21:6]).

Jesus tells the disciples that for a short time they will not see him, and that they will weep and mourn while the world rejoices, but their sorrow will be turned to joy – a clear parallel to the longing to see the Son of Man ([ref:Joh 16:16-22|John 16:16-22]).

The prophet Amos warns those who long for the day of the Lord, for it will be darkness and not light – an Old Testament parallel to the warning against longing for the day of the Son of Man ([ref:Am 5:18-20|Amos 5:18-20]).

The further context in Luke 17 elaborates on what the days of the Son of Man entail, with reference to the days of Noah and Lot, showing that it is judgment and the final return Jesus refers to ([ref:Luk 17:26-30|Luke 17:26-30]).

Matthew's parallel words that people will say "Look, here is Christ" or "there", and that the coming of the Son of Man will be like lightning, complement Jesus' warning to the disciples about longing for his return ([ref:Matt 24:23-27|Matthew 24:23-27]).

The faithful witnesses in the Old Testament lived in longing for the fulfillment of God's promises without seeing them fulfilled – a parallel to the disciples' longing for the day of the Son of Man ([ref:Hebr 11:13-16|Hebrews 11:13-16]).

Peter warns that in the last days there will come scoffers who ask where the promise of Jesus' return has gone, reflecting the enduring longing and waiting that Jesus speaks about ([ref:2 Pet 3:3-4|2 Peter 3:3-4]).
